content: Nitroglycerin is a medication prescribed to prevent chest pain, also known as angina. It achieves this by relaxing the blood vessels in the heart, which increases blood flow and oxygen supply to the heart muscle. This medication may also be prescribed for other conditions, so consult your doctor or pharmacist for additional information. Nitroglycerin is available in several forms, including sublingual tablets, buccal tablets, extended-release capsules, and sprays for oral use. The buccal and extended-release tablets or capsules are typically taken three to six times daily. It is important not to crush, chew, or divide the extended-release forms. Buccal extended-release tablets can also be used during an angina attack or just before activities that may provoke one. Follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully, and ask your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Take nitroglycerin exactly as prescribed. Do not take more or less of it, or take it more frequently than directed by your doctor. While nitroglycerin helps control chest pain, it does not cure the condition. Continue taking the medication even if you feel well, and do not stop using it without consulting your doctor. Abruptly stopping nitroglycerin may lead to chest pain. Over time, the medication may become less effective, a phenomenon known as tolerance. If your angina attacks become more frequent, last longer, or are more severe, contact your doctor immediately. If you are using buccal extended-release tablets, place the tablet between your cheek and gum and allow it to dissolve. Do not chew or swallow the tablet. If you feel dizzy, sit down after placing the tablet in your mouth. Avoid swallowing saliva until the tablet has completely dissolved. Buccal extended-release tablets typically begin working within two to three minutes. To speed up the dissolution process, you can touch the tablet with your tongue before placing it in your mouth or drink a hot liquid. If an angina attack occurs while you have a buccal tablet in place, you may place a second tablet on the opposite side of your mouth. If chest pain persists, use sublingual tablets, call for emergency assistance, or go to the nearest hospital emergency department immediately. For acute chest pain, always carry sublingual tablets or spray with you. Sit down when an attack occurs. Sublingual tablets and sprays typically begin working within two minutes and provide relief for up to 30 minutes. If chest pain is not relieved within five minutes after taking a sublingual tablet, take another dose. If using the spray, repeat the process if pain persists after three to five minutes. If you have taken three tablets (at five-minute intervals) or used three sprays (at threeto five-minute intervals) and 15 minutes have passed without relief, call for emergency assistance or go to the hospital immediately. To use sublingual tablets, place one under your tongue or between your cheek and gum and allow it to dissolve. Do not swallow the tablet, and try to avoid swallowing saliva until the tablet has dissolved. To use the spray, do not shake the container. Hold it upright with the spray mechanism close to your open mouth. Press the spray mechanism with your forefinger to release the medication, spraying it onto or under your tongue. Close your mouth immediately after spraying. Do not inhale or swallow the spray. Nitroglycerin is also used in combination with other medications to treat congestive heart failure and heart attacks. Discuss the potential risks and benefits of using this medication for your condition with your doctor. Before taking nitroglycerin, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to nitroglycerin, isosorbide, or any other medications. Provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription medications you are taking, including aspirin, beta blockers, calcium channel blockers, dihydroergotamine, sildenafil, and vitamins. Notify your doctor if you have anemia, glaucoma, or a history of recent head trauma. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. If you become pregnant while taking nitroglycerin, contact your doctor immediately. If you are scheduled for surgery, including dental procedures, inform your healthcare provider that you are taking nitroglycerin. Be aware that this medication may cause drowsiness or dizziness, so avoid driving or operating machinery until you know how it affects you. Ask your doctor about the safe consumption of alcohol while taking nitroglycerin, as alcohol can exacerbate the medication's side effects. Take extended-release tablets and capsules on an empty stomach with a full glass of water. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one. Common side effects of nitroglycerin include headaches, rash, dizziness, upset stomach, and flushing. If these symptoms are severe or persistent, inform your doctor. Serious side effects, such as blurred vision, dry mouth, chest pain, or fainting, require immediate medical attention. You or your doctor may report serious side effects to the FDA's MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program. Store nitroglycerin in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from excess heat and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Avoid puncturing the spray container and keep it away from heat sources. Do not open a container of sublingual tablets until you need a dose, and discard any tablets that are more than 12 months old. Dispose of outdated or unused medication properly, and consult your pharmacist if you have questions about disposal. In case of overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual has collapsed or is not breathing, call 911 immediately. Keep all appointments with your doctor and any recommended laboratory tests. Extended-release capsules should not be used for acute angina attacks; continue using sublingual tablets or spray for immediate relief. If headaches persist, consult your doctor about taking acetaminophen. Do not take aspirin or other headache medications unless directed by your doctor. Sublingual tablets may cause a sweet, tingling sensation when placed under the tongue, but the absence of this sensation does not indicate that the medication is ineffective. Do not share your medication with others, and consult your pharmacist if you have questions about refilling your prescription. Nitroglycerin is available under several brand names, including Nitro-Bid®, Nitrogard®, Nitroglycerin Slocaps®, Nitrolingual® Pumpspray, NitroQuick®, Nitrostat®, Nitrotab®, and Nitro-Time®.
